cards.title: Cumulative Capstone Review & Practical Laboratory Guide
body: 4.1 Scientific Method and Laboratory Safety in Chemistry

Scientific inquiry in chemistry is a systematic method of investigating the material world through controlled observation, hypothesis formulation, rigorous laboratory experimentation, and data analysis.

To safely and successfully study the transformations of matter, chemists must operate in a highly controlled environment: the laboratory. Laboratory chemistry is fundamentally different from theoretical study; it requires active hands-on experimentation, precise measurements, and strict adherence to safety protocols. Before starting any practical chemistry experiment, a student must become familiar with basic laboratory safety rules. These include wearing personal protective equipment (PPE)—specifically safety goggles, a lab coat, and closed-toe shoes—at all times to prevent chemical splashes on the skin or in the eyes. Working in a chemistry laboratory also requires absolute discipline: one must never eat, drink, or taste chemicals, and nose-smelling of gases must always be done using the proper 'wafting' technique to avoid inhaling toxic vapors.

In addition to safety, executing the scientific method in the laboratory requires utilizing specialized chemical apparatus. Each piece of glassware is designed for a specific purpose. For instance, beakers and Erlenmeyer flasks are used for mixing and holding liquids, but they are not accurate enough for measuring precise volumes. For quantitative measurements, chemists use graduated cylinders, volumetric pipettes, or burettes. Heating substances is commonly achieved using a Bunsen burner, which burns a mixture of gas and air to produce an adjustable hot blue flame. Heating volatile or flammable organic liquids must never be done over an open flame; instead, a water bath or a hot plate must be used.

cards.title: Lab / review
cards.problem: Which of the following represents the safest technique to smell an unknown gas generated during a laboratory experiment?

steps.text: Inhaling directly over a reaction vessel can cause severe respiratory damage from toxic vapors.
The standardized safe method is to hold the vessel a few inches away and wave or **waft** the vapors toward the nose with a hand.

cards.answer: Use your hand to gently waft the vapors toward your nose from a safe distance.

cards.title: Lab / review
cards.problem: When reading the liquid volume in a glass graduated cylinder, at which position should your eyes be aligned, and which part of the meniscus should be read?

steps.text: Viewing from above or below causes parallax errors in volume measurements.
To get an accurate volumetric measurement, your eyes must be directly level with the liquid surface, and you must read the value at the very **bottom of the meniscus curve**.

cards.answer: Look at eye level and read the bottom of the curved meniscus.

cards.title: Lab / review
cards.problem: Which of the following subatomic particles is located outside the atomic nucleus and carries a unit negative electrical charge?

steps.text: Protons and neutrons reside inside the positive nucleus. Electrons revolve around the nucleus in shells.
Electrons carry a unit negative charge ($$-1$$).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following represents the safest technique to smell an unknown gas generated during a laboratory experiment?

options.A: Inhale deeply with your nose positioned directly over the test tube opening.
options.B: Use your hand to gently waft the vapors toward your nose from a safe distance.
options.C: Taste a small liquid droplet of the reaction mixture.
options.D: Suction the gas into a syringe and inject it toward your face.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand laboratory gas smelling safety**
Inhaling directly over a reaction vessel can cause severe respiratory damage from toxic vapors.

**Step 2: Identify the correct technique**
The standardized safe method is to hold the vessel a few inches away and wave or **waft** the vapors toward the nose with a hand.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct option is **Use your hand to gently waft the vapors toward your nose from a safe distance**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When reading the liquid volume in a glass graduated cylinder, at which position should your eyes be aligned, and which part of the meniscus should be read?

options.A: Look from above and read the top edge of the meniscus.
options.B: Look at eye level and read the bottom of the curved meniscus.
options.C: Look from below and read the top edge of the meniscus.
options.D: Look at any angle and read the average of the top and bottom values.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand volume measurement guidelines**
Viewing from above or below causes parallax errors in volume measurements.

**Step 2: Locate the meniscus reading point**
To get an accurate volumetric measurement, your eyes must be directly level with the liquid surface, and you must read the value at the very **bottom of the meniscus curve**.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
Therefore, the correct choice is to **look at eye level and read the bottom of the curved meniscus**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following subatomic particles is located outside the atomic nucleus and carries a unit negative electrical charge?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify locations of subatomic particles**
Protons and neutrons reside inside the positive nucleus. Electrons revolve around the nucleus in shells.

**Step 2: Identify charge characteristics**
Electrons carry a unit negative charge ($$-1$$).

**Step 3: Conclusion**
Therefore, the particle is the **Electron**.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus measures 25.0 cm³ of a solution most accurately?
questions.label: 1. Which piece of apparatus measures 25.0 cm³ of a solution most accurately?

similar.q: Which apparatus delivers variable volumes accurately in a titration?
Is a graduated cylinder more or less accurate than a pipette?

why: Answer C: Volumetric pipette
Beakers, flasks and test tubes have rough or no volume marks.
A volumetric pipette is calibrated to deliver one fixed volume very precisely.
So use a 25.0 cm³ volumetric pipette.

questions.q: How should you heat a flammable liquid such as ethanol in the laboratory?
questions.label: 2. How should you heat a flammable liquid such as ethanol in the laboratory?

similar.q: Why must closed containers never be heated?
similar.a: Pressure builds up and they can explode.

similar.q: Name the flame used for strong heating.

options.A: With a match held under the beaker
options.B: In a water bath or on a hot plate
options.C: In a closed container over a flame

why: Answer B: In a water bath or on a hot plate
Flammable vapours can catch fire from an open flame.
A water bath or hot plate heats without a naked flame.
Never heat a closed container – pressure can make it burst.

questions.label: 3. True or false: You should look down into a test tube while heating it to see the reaction clearly.

similar.q: Which way should a heated test tube point?
What protects your eyes in the lab?

why: False. Heated liquids can spit or boil over suddenly.
Always point the mouth of the test tube away from yourself and others.
Observe from the side, wearing safety goggles.

questions.q: When reading a measuring cylinder containing water, you should read ____.
questions.label: 4. When reading a measuring cylinder containing water, you should read ____.

similar.q: What error is caused by reading from an angle?
For mercury, which part of the meniscus is read?

options.A: the bottom of the meniscus at eye level
options.B: the top of the meniscus from above
options.D: the edge of the glass from below

why: Answer A: the bottom of the meniscus at eye level
Water forms a curved surface (meniscus) that dips in the middle.
Reading from above or below gives a parallax error.
Put your eye level with the surface and read the bottom of the curve.

questions.q: A Bunsen burner gives a yellow, smoky flame. What should you do to get a hot blue flame?
questions.label: 5. A Bunsen burner gives a yellow, smoky flame. What should you do to get a hot blue flame?

similar.q: Which flame is safer when the burner is not in use?
similar.a: The yellow flame, because it is easy to see.

similar.q: Which flame is hotter?

why: Answer D: Open the air hole
A yellow (luminous) flame means too little air: incomplete combustion.
Opening the air hole lets more air mix with the gas.
Complete combustion gives a hot, clean blue flame.

questions.q: What is the first thing to do if a chemical splashes into your eye?
questions.label: 6. What is the first thing to do if a chemical splashes into your eye?

similar.q: Why should you not rub the eye?
similar.a: It spreads the chemical and can scratch the eye.

similar.q: Name one piece of PPE for the body.

options.A: Rinse the eye with plenty of running water and tell the teacher
options.B: Add another chemical to neutralise it

why: Answer A: Rinse the eye with plenty of running water and tell the teacher
Speed matters: flush the chemical out at once.
Rinse with plenty of clean running water (eyewash) for several minutes.
Report to the teacher; never add another chemical.

questions.q: In the scientific method, a testable prediction that explains an observation is called a ____.
questions.label: 7. In the scientific method, a testable prediction that explains an observation is called a ____.

similar.q: What do we call the factor that is deliberately changed?
Why do we keep other factors constant?

why: Answer D: hypothesis
The method: observe → ask a question → form a hypothesis → experiment → analyse → conclude.
A hypothesis is a testable explanation or prediction.
Experiments then support or reject it.

questions.q: Which method separates salt from salt solution?
questions.label: 8. Which method separates salt from salt solution?

similar.q: Which method separates sand from water?
Which method collects pure water from salt water?

why: Answer B: Evaporation
Salt is dissolved, so it passes through filter paper.
Heating evaporates the water and leaves the salt behind.
Magnets and decanting do not separate a dissolved solid.

questions.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.label: 9. Which of these is a chemical change?

similar.q: Give one sign of a chemical change.
similar.a: Gas given off / colour change / heat or light produced.

similar.q: Is boiling water a chemical change?
similar.a: No, it is a physical change.

why: Answer B: Burning wood
A chemical change makes a new substance and is hard to reverse.
Burning wood produces ash, carbon dioxide and water.
Melting, dissolving and crushing only change state or size.

questions.q: An atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons. What is its mass number?
questions.label: 10. An atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons. What is its mass number?

similar.q: What is its atomic number?
Which element is it?

why: Answer A: 23
Mass number = protons + neutrons.
Electrons have almost no mass and are not counted.

questions.q: Isotopes of an element have the same number of ____ but different numbers of ____.
questions.label: 11. Isotopes of an element have the same number of ____ but different numbers of ____.

similar.q: How many neutrons does carbon-14 have?
Do isotopes have the same chemical properties?

why: Answer A: protons; neutrons
The number of protons fixes the element.
Isotopes differ only in neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.
Example: carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons.

questions.q: What is the electron arrangement of an atom with 17 electrons?
questions.label: 12. What is the electron arrangement of an atom with 17 electrons?

similar.q: Electron arrangement of magnesium (12 electrons)?
How many valence electrons does chlorine have?

why: Answer B: 2, 8, 7
Fill shells in order: first shell up to 2, second up to 8, then the third.
Arrangement 2, 8, 7 (chlorine).

questions.q: Which particle has a negative charge and is found in shells around the nucleus?
questions.label: 13. Which particle has a negative charge and is found in shells around the nucleus?

similar.q: Which particle has no charge?
Relative mass of a proton?

why: Answer D: Electron
Protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) are in the nucleus.
Electrons (−1) move in shells around it.
So the answer is the electron.

questions.q: What is the correct formula of aluminium oxide? (Al³⁺, O²⁻)
questions.label: 14. What is the correct formula of aluminium oxide? (Al³⁺, O²⁻)

similar.q: Formula of magnesium chloride (Mg²⁺, Cl⁻)?
Formula of sodium oxide (Na⁺, O²⁻)?

why: Answer D: Al₂O₃
Charges must balance: Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
Lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6: 2 Al³⁺ = +6 and 3 O²⁻ = −6.
Formula Al₂O₃.

questions.q: Which equation is balanced?
questions.label: 15. Which equation is balanced?

similar.q: Balance: Mg + O₂ → MgO.
Balance: N₂ + H₂ → NH₃.

why: Answer A: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Count atoms on each side.
2H₂ + O₂: 4 H and 2 O; 2H₂O: 4 H and 2 O – equal.
The other equations have unequal numbers of H or O atoms.

questions.q: How many atoms are in one formula unit of CaCO₃?
questions.label: 16. How many atoms are in one formula unit of CaCO₃?

similar.q: How many oxygen atoms are in 2H₂SO₄?
How many atoms in H₂O?

why: Answer D: 5
CaCO₃ contains 1 Ca, 1 C and 3 O.
Subscripts count the atom immediately before them.

questions.label: 17. The symbol of potassium is ____.

similar.q: Symbol of sodium and its Latin name?
Symbol of iron?

why: Answer D: K
Some symbols come from Latin names.
Potassium comes from "kalium", so its symbol is K.
P is phosphorus, Po polonium and Pt platinum.

questions.q: True or false: A mixture can be separated by physical methods, but a compound cannot.
questions.label: 18. True or false: A mixture can be separated by physical methods, but a compound cannot.

similar.q: Is air a mixture or a compound?
Is water a mixture or a compound?

why: True. In a mixture the substances are not chemically joined.
Filtration, evaporation or distillation can separate them.
A compound's elements are chemically bonded and need a chemical reaction to separate.

questions.q: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
questions.label: 19. Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?

similar.q: Which state is easiest to compress?
What is the change from gas to liquid called?

why: Answer D: Liquid
Solids keep both shape and volume.
Gases fill their container: no fixed shape or volume.
Liquids keep their volume but take the shape of the container.
